strengths: Novel hierarchical MAB formulation for kernel optimization that naturally decomposes the problem into kernel selection and strategy selection
Principled algorithmic framework seamlessly integrating profiling-guided strategy selection, runtime behavior clustering, and hierarchical UCB with O(K√T ln T) regret bound
Comprehensive experiments across multiple configurations (2 hardware platforms, 2 LLM backends) showing consistent and substantial improvements (2-9× speedup)
Sustained scalability demonstrated through extended optimization trajectories (20 iterations) where KERNELBAND continues improving while baselines saturate
Well-motivated design addressing distinctive challenges (non-stationary rewards, contextual effectiveness, large action space, expensive evaluations)
Rigorous evaluation methodology using TritonBench's framework with multi-shape testing, correctness verification, and statistical robustness

weaknesses: Critical limitation: only compared against GEAK baseline; no experiments with STARK, EvoEngineer, ConCuR, Kevin, or TritonRL mentioned in related work, making it impossible to assess whether improvements stem from hierarchical MAB formulation or other algorithmic factors

Key design choices lack principled justification: K=3 clusters chosen via empirical observation without ablation; α=0.5 parameter weight set arbitrarily without sensitivity analysis; clustering update frequency (Δ=10) unexplained

Missing critical ablations: no ablation on α weighting, number of clusters K, profiling feature sets, or UCB term contributions; insufficient justification for feature engineering choices (why these 9 dimensions for ϕ and 6 for ρ)
Reward function r∈(-∞,1] exhibits problematic asymmetry (unbounded downside) contradicting standard UCB analysis assumptions of bounded [0,1] rewards; impact on convergence analysis unexplored
Method appears specialized to Triton kernels; generalization to CUDA, HIP, or other frameworks unexplored despite claiming broader applicability
Limited analysis depth: case study covers only one kernel (seeded_dropout); no investigation of failure modes or scenarios where KERNELBAND underperforms compared to GEAK

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation casting kernel optimization as hierarchical multi-armed bandit with natural exploration-exploitation structure
Hardware-aware design integrating performance counters via logistic regression to guide strategy selection
Theoretical contribution providing regret bounds O(K|S|√T log T) with cluster-based complexity reduction
Multi-platform evaluation across consumer (RTX 4090) and datacenter (A100) GPUs with two LLM backends demonstrating some generality
Clear presentation of motivation, problem formulation, algorithm design, and comprehensive algorithm description
Practical combination of profiling guidance, runtime clustering, and UCB that addresses real optimization challenges
weaknesses: Critical limitation: Only single baseline (GEAK) compared; no comparisons with STARK, EvoEngineer, ConCuR, Kevin, CUDA-L1, TritonRL, or basic baselines (random search, vanilla UCB, Thompson Sampling)

Experimental instability demonstrated by high variance (e.g., Table 1 GPT-5.1 showing 0.88-11.19 speedup swings); unclear if results are reliable or cherry-picked by metric selection

Methodological design unjustified: Hand-crafted features (9-dim profiling, 6-dim runtime) lack ablation or sensitivity analysis; clustering hyperparameters (Δ=10, refresh on |C_t| doubling) appear arbitrary; logistic regression choices (B=500 buffer, η=0.1, λ=10^-4) unchosen empirically

Limited benchmark scope: Only 29 TritonBench kernels (one excluded due to 'anomalous speedup' without investigation); no real ML workloads; no out-of-distribution testing; raises concern about method generalization

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation across two distinct GPU platforms (consumer/datacenter), two LLM backends (open-source/commercial), and 29 diverse kernels with multi-shape testing and statistical robustness

Superior scalability without saturation: extended experiments show KERNELBAND continues improving through 20 iterations while GEAK plateaus around iteration 10
Rigorous evaluation methodology following TritonBench framework with correctness verification, multi-shape evaluation, and weighted aggregation of results

Limited scope: Evaluation restricted to GPU kernels via Triton; generalization to other accelerators or languages unclear; single benchmark (TritonBench) tested

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation identifying a fundamental mismatch between LLM code generation and kernel optimization as an exploration-exploitation problem

Rigorous ablation studies convincingly demonstrate the bandit policy is essential (regression to 0.97× without it), validating the core contribution
Evidence of hardware-aware adaptation with platform-specific strategy selection patterns (Table 10, Appendix I), supporting the hardware-informed design
Comprehensive evaluation on 183 kernels with well-designed metrics, careful correctness verification protocols, and cost efficiency analysis
Theoretical contribution providing a regret bound dependent on compact covering number K|S_valid| rather than unbounded kernel space, with rigorous decomposition proof

weaknesses: Critical assumptions lack empirical validation: Assumption 2 (Lipschitz continuity) is never verified empirically—no measurement of the Lipschitz constant L or evidence that strategy effectiveness varies smoothly with kernel behavior; Assumption 1's bounding function B(k,s) is heuristic without theoretical justification

Limited baseline comparisons: only GEAK and weak Best-of-N compared; concurrent methods (STARK, TritonForge, CudaForge) unavailable, making it difficult to isolate whether improvements come from the MAB formulation specifically
